body: There is a completely valid reason the compiler complains currently, and that is nonstandard inheritance (`virtual` and multiple inheritance). I learned about this whole mess recently in [Arthur O'Dwyer's CppCon 2017 talk](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=QzJL-8WbpuU): For the normal, linear inheritance we know and love, `SomeSubType * == SomeSuperType *` because `SomeSuperType` things are inserted before `SomeSubType` things, so the pointer can simply be reinterpreted. However, this assumption doesn't hold in more complex subclassing setups. For example, it may not be true for virtual bases where the super struct can be inserted elsewhere into the full struct: However, our `Object` does not support virtual or multiple bases anyway, and I can't think of a reason why we should consider supporting it. This kind of complex subclassing logic just isn't needed most times. So I think it's perfectly fine to make the assumption of linear inheritance you're making here. Edit: It might be worth it making a follow-up PR that statically asserts this assumption, to make sure nobody attempts to do virtual or multiple inheritance to `Object` in the future. Not sure how that would be achievable off the top of my head though.
